Two approaches to completion tracking: fixed completions (set completions equal to queue depth, each pod processes one item and exits 0) — works when the queue depth is known before the Job starts; and queue-drain termination (set completions: 1, parallelism: N, workers exit 0 only when they observe an empty queue) — works for dynamic queue sizes. The Indexed Job mode (completionMode: Indexed, GA in 1.24) assigns each pod a stable integer index via the JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX environment variable, enabling sharded processing without an external queue (each worker processes its index's slice of data deterministically). Worker idempotency is the critical design constraint: because pods can be interrupted by preemption, node failure, or OOM, every task must be safe to process twice. The standard contract is claim-process-acknowledge: a worker claims a task (making it invisible to others), processes it, and only acknowledges (commits/deletes) from the queue after processing is confirmed complete. Claiming without acknowledging on crash causes the message to return to the queue after the visibility timeout. Redis, RabbitMQ, and SQS all implement this pattern; Kafka uses consumer group offsets instead.
words.connector: Think of the work queue pattern like a self-checkout register bank at a grocery store — shoppers (tasks) queue up, any available register (worker pod) takes the next shopper, processes their items independently, and the next shopper advances. The checkout manager (scheduler) can add more registers if the queue grows long.
words.techContext: Our nightly image-processing pipeline uses a Redis work queue: a CronJob pushes 50,000 image IDs at midnight, and a Job with parallelism: 20 drains the queue by 3 AM, with any interrupted items automatically retried by other workers.
words.exampleSentence: When three workers crashed simultaneously due to a node failure mid-batch, their unclaimed Redis tasks were automatically re-queued after the visibility timeout and processed by surviving workers — not a single image was lost.

codeExample.code:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: image-processor
spec:
  parallelism: 8            # 8 concurrent workers
  completions: 8            # total completions required
  completionMode: Indexed   # each pod gets a stable index
  backoffLimit: 4
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: my-image-processor:1.0
        env:
        - name: REDIS_URL
          value: redis://redis-svc:6379
        - name: WORKER_INDEX
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.annotations['batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index']

words.etymology: Work from Old English weorc ('labor, deed') + queue from French queue ('tail, line') — a line of work to be processed. Pattern from Latin patronus ('model, example') — a reusable solution template. The compound describes a recurring architectural approach for parallel batch processing.

words.shortDefinition: The CNCF-graduated container runtime that kubelet communicates with via CRI to manage image pulls, overlay snapshots, and container process lifecycle.
words.simpleDefinition: containerd is the container runtime that actually runs containers on every Kubernetes node. kubelet does not talk to Docker (Docker was removed in Kubernetes 1.24); it talks to containerd via the Container Runtime Interface (CRI). containerd handles image pulling from registries, unpacking OCI image layers into overlay filesystems (snapshots), starting and stopping container processes (via runc as the default OCI runtime), and managing container logs. It is the default runtime on GKE, EKS, AKS, and most production Kubernetes distributions.
words.longDefinition: containerd was extracted from Docker (as the lower-level runtime) in 2017 and donated to the CNCF, graduating in 2019. It follows a layered architecture: containerd itself manages the high-level lifecycle (image management, container metadata, task scheduling); it delegates actual process execution to a shimv2-based OCI runtime (default: runc, alternatives: kata-agent for Kata Containers, runsc for gVisor). The shim layer decouples containerd's lifecycle from the container process — if containerd restarts, the shim keeps the container running and re-attaches. The CRI plugin built into containerd (since 1.1) allows kubelet to communicate via the CRI gRPC interface without an intermediate adapter. containerd uses a plugin architecture: you can enable or disable features (CRI, snapshotter, garbage collector) and configure them independently. The snapshotter manages the layered filesystem: for each container, containerd creates a read-write overlay layer on top of the image's read-only layers (using overlayfs, zfs, or other backends). containerd also hosts the nerdctl CLI (Docker-compatible command-line tool) and is increasingly used directly in serverless runtimes (AWS Lambda, Fargate) for its lightweight footprint.
words.connector: Think of containerd like the logistics engine of a shipping company — it manages the warehouse (image storage), coordinates the loading dock (image pulls from registry), and dispatches delivery drivers (runc processes) to move containers to their destinations, all without being the truck driver itself.
words.techContext: After the Docker shim deprecation, we updated our CI/CD pipelines to use nerdctl (the containerd-native CLI) for local image builds and debugged a cni plugin issue by inspecting containerd's snapshot metadata directly.
words.exampleSentence: The node was failing to pull large images because the containerd snapshot store was full — clearing the dangling snapshots with ctr snapshot rm freed 40 GB and restored scheduling capacity.

codeExample.code:
# List running containers via containerd's CLI
sudo ctr containers list

# List images cached by containerd
sudo ctr images list

# Pull an image directly through containerd
sudo ctr images pull docker.io/library/nginx:1.25

# Inspect containerd config and CRI plugin status
sudo crictl info | jq '.config.containerdEndpoint'

words.etymology: A portmanteau of 'container' + 'd' (Unix daemon suffix). The name signals its role as the background daemon service managing container lifecycle, analogous to systemd or Docker's dockerd.

words.shortDefinition: A hidden infrastructure container started by kubelet as the first container in every pod to hold the pod's network namespace, ensuring container restarts do not change the pod's IP address.
words.simpleDefinition: Every Kubernetes pod contains at least one container you did not ask for: the pause container (also called the infra container). It runs a minimal binary that does nothing except sleep forever, holding open the Linux network namespace. All other containers in the pod join this network namespace — they share the IP and port space. If an app container crashes and restarts, a new process starts in the same namespace, keeping the pod's IP stable. Without the pause container, a container restart would create a new network namespace with a new IP, breaking in-flight connections and kube-proxy routing.
words.longDefinition: The pause container image (gcr.io/pause, registry.k8s.io/pause) is a ~250KB binary written in C that calls pause() (a POSIX syscall that suspends the process until a signal arrives) in an infinite loop. Its sole purpose is to be the namespace holder. When kubelet creates a pod, it creates the pause container first (via CRI), gets its PID and network namespace, then creates each app container joined to that namespace (using the --net=container:<pause-id> semantic at the CRI layer). The pause container also holds the IPC namespace (enabling shared memory between pod containers) and the UTS namespace (hostname). Because it holds the namespaces, even if all app containers in the pod die and are restarted, the namespace files (/proc/<pause-pid>/ns/net) remain open and the pod's IP is preserved in the cluster's routing tables. In managed Kubernetes services, the pause image version is managed by the control plane; self-managed clusters set it via kubelet's --pod-infra-container-image flag. Admission webhooks and container scanning tools sometimes need to explicitly exclude the pause container from scanning, as it intentionally has no filesystem content to scan.
words.connector: Think of the pause container like a permanent mailbox installed at an address — the actual mail-carriers (app containers) come and go, get replaced when they quit, but the mailbox stays at the address permanently so mail (network traffic) always knows where to go.
words.techContext: Our container security scanner falsely flagged the pause container as vulnerable-to-scan-skipped because it has no file layer; we added a registry exception for registry.k8s.io/pause to avoid alert fatigue.
words.exampleSentence: When all three app containers in a pod crashed simultaneously due to an OOM event, the pod's IP remained stable throughout the restart because the pause container kept the network namespace alive while kubelet recreated the app containers.

codeExample.code:
# Pause containers are visible in containerd but not in kubectl
sudo crictl ps --all | grep pause
# You'll see one pause container per pod on the node

# Inspect the pause container's network namespace
PAUSE_PID=$(sudo crictl inspect <pause-container-id> | jq -r '.info.pid')
sudo nsenter --net=/proc/$PAUSE_PID/ns/net ip addr show

words.etymology: Pause from Latin pausare ('to stop, halt') — named for the pause() system call its binary executes indefinitely. Container from Latin continere ('to hold together') — it holds the shared namespaces together for the pod.

words.shortDefinition: A CRD-and-controller pair that encrypts Kubernetes Secrets with a cluster-held asymmetric key so the encrypted form can be safely committed to Git.
words.simpleDefinition: Sealed Secrets solves a fundamental GitOps problem: Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded (not encrypted), so committing them to Git exposes credentials. The Sealed Secrets controller generates an asymmetric key pair and stores the private key in the cluster. You use the kubeseal CLI to encrypt a Secret with the cluster's public key, producing a SealedSecret CRD object. This encrypted object is safe to commit to Git — only the specific cluster with the matching private key can decrypt it. The controller watches for SealedSecret objects, decrypts them, and creates the corresponding native Kubernetes Secret.
words.longDefinition: Sealed Secrets was created by Bitnami (now part of VMware/Broadcom) and is a popular open-source project. The encryption uses hybrid cryptography: the Secret's plaintext is encrypted with a random AES key (symmetric, fast), and the AES key itself is encrypted with the cluster's RSA-4096 public key (asymmetric, slow but used only once per seal). The output SealedSecret CRD stores the ciphertext and the encrypted AES key. The controller's private key is stored as a regular Kubernetes Secret in the kube-system namespace — protecting it (RBAC, etcd encryption) is critical for the overall security model. Key rotation: the controller generates a new key pair every 30 days by default; old sealed secrets encrypted with previous keys remain decryptable (old private keys are retained). The scope field on a SealedSecret binds decryption to a specific namespace or even a specific Secret name, preventing a sealed secret intended for one namespace from being copied to another. Sealed Secrets is designed for teams using GitOps (Argo CD, Flux) where all cluster resources live in Git — SealedSecrets are the one mechanism that makes this practical for credentials without a separate secrets manager infrastructure.
words.connector: Think of Sealed Secrets like a safety deposit box at a bank: you put your valuables (the Secret plaintext) into the box (encrypt with the public key), and only the bank vault (the controller with the private key) can open it — you can share the locked box freely without exposing its contents.
words.techContext: Our entire infrastructure is GitOps with Argo CD; we commit SealedSecret objects alongside all other manifests, and the Sealed Secrets controller decrypts them at apply time — no secrets manager infrastructure required for teams starting out.
words.exampleSentence: After adopting Sealed Secrets, our Git history no longer required secret branches or manual encryption steps — database passwords are committed as SealedSecret YAML objects alongside the Deployment that uses them.

codeExample.code:
# Fetch the cluster's public key
kubeseal --fetch-cert \
  --controller-namespace kube-system \
  --controller-name sealed-secrets-controller \
  > pub-sealed-secrets.pem

# Seal a secret
kubectl create secret generic db-password \
  --dry-run=client \
  --from-literal=password='s3cr3t' \
  -o yaml | \
  kubeseal --cert pub-sealed-secrets.pem \
  -o yaml > sealed-db-password.yaml

# Commit sealed-db-password.yaml to Git safely

words.etymology: Sealed from Old English seglian ('to mark with a seal') — in cryptography, sealing means encrypting in a way only the key-holder can unseal. Secrets from Latin secretus ('set apart, hidden'). The compound describes secrets made safe for storage by asymmetric encryption.

words.shortDefinition: A lifecycle hook that runs synchronously before SIGTERM is sent to a container, used to bridge the load-balancer-deregistration race condition during pod termination.
words.simpleDefinition: When Kubernetes deletes a pod, two events happen in parallel: the endpoints controller removes the pod's IP from Service endpoints (propagating to kube-proxy on all nodes), and kubelet begins the termination sequence. The propagation takes 1-5 seconds, but SIGTERM arrives immediately. During that window, the load balancer still routes new connections to the pod — which may have already closed its listener. The preStop hook bridges this gap: it runs before SIGTERM is sent, its duration consumes from the terminationGracePeriodSeconds budget, and a 5-second sleep in the hook gives the control plane time to drain traffic before the application begins shutting down.
words.longDefinition: The preStop hook is defined under spec.containers[].lifecycle.preStop and supports the same handler types as probes: exec (run a shell command), httpGet (call an HTTP endpoint), and sleep (Kubernetes 1.29+ — native sleep without needing /bin/sleep in the image). The hook is synchronous: kubelet waits for the hook to complete (or for terminationGracePeriodSeconds to expire, whichever comes first) before sending SIGTERM. The hook duration consumes from the shared terminationGracePeriodSeconds budget — if the budget is 30 seconds and the preStop hook takes 5 seconds, the application has 25 seconds to drain connections and exit after SIGTERM arrives. The race condition the preStop hook solves: kubelet sends SIGTERM to the container process; if the application immediately closes its listener on SIGTERM (correct behavior), new connections routed to the pod's IP during the kube-proxy propagation window get connection-refused. A preStop sleep of 5-10 seconds holds the container alive long enough for kube-proxy to update its iptables rules and the load balancer to stop routing to the pod. This pattern is a best practice for any HTTP service that handles rolling updates or node drains gracefully. Without it, you will see 502/503 errors during rolling deployments even if the application handles SIGTERM correctly.
words.connector: Think of the preStop hook like the announcement before a restaurant closes: 'Last orders please — we stop serving in 5 minutes.' It gives customers (in-flight requests) time to finish, the kitchen (app) time to serve them, and the front door (load balancer) time to stop letting new customers in — all before the lights go off.
words.techContext: Adding a 10-second preStop sleep eliminated the 502 error spike we were seeing during every rolling deployment — those errors disappeared because kube-proxy had time to drain the pod from all iptables rules before the app stopped accepting connections.
words.exampleSentence: The SRE team traced 0.3% of rolling-deploy requests returning 503 to a missing preStop hook — after adding preStop: sleep: seconds: 5, the error rate dropped to zero during deployments.

codeExample.code:
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60  # total budget
  containers:
  - name: api
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        sleep:
          seconds: 10   # K8s 1.29+ native sleep
        # Older clusters:
        # exec:
        #   command: ["/bin/sleep", "10"]
    # Application has ~50s to drain after SIGTERM

words.etymology: Pre- from Latin prae ('before') + stop from Old English stoppian ('to close'). Hook from Old English hoc ('bent object') — a hook is a handler that attaches to a specific event in a lifecycle. The compound describes a handler that runs before the stop signal.

words.shortDefinition: kube-proxy operating mode that uses Linux IP Virtual Server hash tables for O(1) Service routing, superseding iptables at clusters with 1000+ Services.
words.simpleDefinition: kube-proxy has two primary modes for implementing Kubernetes Service routing: iptables (the default) and IPVS. In iptables mode, each Service adds multiple rules to a linear iptables chain — as Services grow into the thousands, lookups become O(N) and rule updates during pod churn become expensive. IPVS mode uses the Linux kernel's IPVS (IP Virtual Server) module, which implements virtual server load balancing using hash tables for O(1) lookups regardless of cluster size. It also provides built-in load-balancing algorithms (round-robin, least connections, source hash) beyond iptables' single random selection.
words.longDefinition: IPVS was originally designed for Linux-based load balancers (LVS — Linux Virtual Server) and uses the Netfilter framework at the INPUT hook, maintaining kernel hash tables of virtual service IPs mapped to real server IPs. kube-proxy in IPVS mode creates an IPVS virtual server for each Kubernetes Service's ClusterIP and populates its real-server table with the pod IPs from EndpointSlices. Route lookups are O(1) (hash table) vs. iptables' O(N) (sequential rule traversal). For a cluster with 10,000 Services, IPVS lookups are thousands of times faster than iptables chains. Updates are also O(1) per change vs. iptables' full-chain rewrite. Enabling IPVS mode requires the ip_vs, ip_vs_rr, ip_vs_sh, and nf_conntrack kernel modules to be loaded on all nodes. IPVS mode requires an additional dummy network interface (kube-ipvs0) to which all ClusterIPs are bound, so the kernel's IPVS module intercepts traffic destined for Service IPs. The caveat: IPVS handles ClusterIP routing, but iptables rules are still used for SNAT/masquerade (NodePort, LoadBalancer) and NetworkPolicy — IPVS mode does not eliminate iptables entirely. In managed Kubernetes services, IPVS is typically enabled by setting kube-proxy's mode: ipvs in the KubeProxyConfiguration.
words.connector: Think of the difference between iptables and IPVS like the difference between a hotel concierge looking up your room assignment in a sequential guest ledger (iptables) versus an instant digital room-key lookup system indexed by your name (IPVS) — both get you to your room, but one scales to a 10,000-room hotel with no degradation.
words.techContext: After upgrading our 500-node cluster to IPVS mode, kube-proxy's CPU usage during node drains dropped by 70% because Service endpoint updates are O(1) hash operations instead of rebuilding iptables chains with thousands of rules.
words.exampleSentence: With 8,000 Services in the cluster, iptables-mode kube-proxy was spending 40% of a core per node just processing rule updates during deployments; switching to IPVS mode brought that to under 2%.

codeExample.code:
# kube-proxy ConfigMap (managed clusters: set via cluster config)
apiVersion: kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: KubeProxyConfiguration
mode: ipvs
ipvs:
  scheduler: "rr"     # round-robin (default)
  # Options: rr, lc (least conn), dh (dest hash), sh (src hash)

# Verify IPVS rules on a node
ipvsadm -Ln | head -30

words.etymology: IPVS from IP Virtual Server — a Linux kernel module implementing virtual server load balancing. Mode from Latin modus ('measure, manner') — the operational manner in which kube-proxy implements Service routing. The compound describes kube-proxy's high-performance routing mode.

words.shortDefinition: A Deployment field requiring a new pod to remain continuously Ready for N seconds before counting as available, slowing rollouts to allow unstable pods to self-reveal.
words.simpleDefinition: minReadySeconds is a Deployment (and StatefulSet, DaemonSet) field that delays counting a newly created pod as 'available' until it has been continuously in the Ready state for at least that many seconds. Without it, a pod counts as available the moment its readiness probe first passes — even if it fails 10 seconds later. With minReadySeconds: 30, a pod that passes readiness then crashes within 30 seconds will not have been counted as available, keeping the rollout from advancing and surfacing the instability early.
words.longDefinition: minReadySeconds defaults to 0, meaning pods are counted as available immediately on first readiness probe success. The field interacts critically with Deployment rolling update strategy: maxUnavailable controls how many old pods can be taken down; maxSurge controls how many new pods can be created above the desired replica count. The rollout advances (taking down old pods or creating new ones) based on the count of 'available' pods. By setting minReadySeconds > 0, you insert a mandatory observation window: a pod must remain Ready for that duration before it contributes to the available count. This catches failure patterns that readiness probes alone miss: a pod that passes readiness on startup but fails due to a slow memory leak, a race condition with a cache warm-up, or a configuration bug that surfaces only after the first request hits a code path not exercised by the health endpoint. A typical value of 30-60 seconds for stateless services catches most transient failures without significantly lengthening rollout duration. For the progress deadline: Kubernetes uses spec.progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600s) to mark a Deployment as stalled if it fails to make progress; minReadySeconds per pod must be less than this deadline or the rollout will always time out. minReadySeconds is often combined with preStop hooks and PodDisruptionBudgets to form a complete rollout safety configuration.
words.connector: Think of minReadySeconds like the probationary period for a new employee before they are counted as a fully productive team member — they may show up and pass orientation (readiness probe), but they only count toward the team's full capacity after they've demonstrated sustained performance for the required probationary window.
words.techContext: Setting minReadySeconds: 60 on our payment service deployment caught a cache-initialization bug where pods passed their readiness probe at second 5 but crashed at second 45 — without the field, the rollout would have proceeded thinking the new pods were healthy.
words.exampleSentence: After adding minReadySeconds: 30, the broken release that had been silently deploying and crashing in a loop was immediately caught as a stalled Deployment because no pod ever stayed Ready for the required 30 seconds.

codeExample.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-server
spec:
  replicas: 5
  minReadySeconds: 30    # pod must stay Ready 30s before counting as available
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0   # zero-downtime: always 5+ available pods
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300   # stall if no progress in 5 min
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          periodSeconds: 5

words.etymology: min from Latin minimus ('smallest, least') + ready from Old English rǣde ('prepared') + seconds from Medieval Latin secunda ('second part, unit of time'). The field name describes the minimum duration a pod must remain in the ready state before the system considers it available.
